result.summary: The gods and the Titans clash in the great war, with Zeus's hundred-handed allies and his thunderbolts shaking the whole cosmos. The Hundred-Handers bury the Titans under rocks and chain them in Tartarus, and the poem then describes Tartarus, the house of Night, and her children Sleep and Death.

scenes.title: The armies meet in battle
scenes.summary: The gods, with the Hundred-Handers whom Zeus brought up from Erebus, face the Titans. The sea, earth, heaven and Tartarus shake at the onset.
scenes.stakes: Both sides risk defeat in the war for rule of the cosmos.

scenes.title: Zeus unleashes his thunderbolts
scenes.summary: Zeus hurls lightning and the world burns and seethes. The Titans are blinded and the battle begins to turn.
scenes.stakes: The Titans face destruction by Zeus's fire.

scenes.title: Titans chained in Tartarus
scenes.summary: The Hundred-Handers bury and bind the Titans beneath the earth. Tartarus is described, with its bronze gates set by Poseidon and its guards.
scenes.stakes: The Titans lose their freedom permanently.

scenes.title: House of Night, Sleep and Death
scenes.summary: Night and Day pass each other at a bronze threshold while Atlas holds up heaven. Night's children Sleep and Death dwell there, one kind to men and the other pitiless.

alias_notes.explanation: Patronymic for Atlas, who holds up heaven; the name is not given in this section.
Variant spelling of the same Hundred-Hander.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable measure of Tartarus's depth by a falling anvil.

analysis.text: Zeus wins sovereignty through force and allies, and the defeated are confined, which establishes the order of the cosmos.
The cosmic geography reflects early Greek ideas of a layered universe with Tartarus as far below earth as heaven is above.

legacy.text: The Titanomachy became a standard subject of Greek and later art and literature, and Tartarus entered later descriptions of the underworld.

fun_facts.text: The falling-anvil measure of nine days is echoed in Homer's Iliad, where Zeus threatens to hurl gods into Tartarus.

language_notes.text: "Givers of good things" is a traditional epithet of the Olympian gods, who are the source of blessings; "he" is Cronos' son Zeus's ally Cottus, who has just spoken.
These are the Hundred-Handers (Cottus, Briareos and Gyes), sons of Heaven and Earth, whom Zeus freed from imprisonment so they would fight for him.
Tartarus is the dark, deep pit far beneath the earth, used as a prison for defeated gods.
"Thunder-stone" means the thunderbolt, imagined as a hurled missile.
Chaos here is the primeval gap or void from which the world began, not mere disorder.
"The battle inclined" means the fight tipped or turned, as a balance does, in favour of one side.
"Insatiate for war" means never satisfied with fighting; the Hundred-Handers are eager for battle. Briareos is also called Obriareus in sentence 20.
A neck-circlet is a collar or necklace; night is pictured as encircling Tartarus the way a collar rings the neck.
"Zeus who drives the clouds" is a stock epithet for Zeus as weather god.
The aegis is Zeus's divine shield or goatskin cloak, which terrified enemies; "warders" are guards.
The son of Iapetus is Atlas, a Titan condemned to hold up the sky. The number 1622 is a stray footnote marker.
"Even evil Night" refers to the Night who stays at home holding Sleep; the phrasing is awkward, and "evil" means baneful rather than morally wicked.

context_notes.text: The Titans, children of Heaven and Earth, ruled before the Olympians. Zeus and his siblings, children of Cronos, are now fighting them for control of the cosmos.
The thunderbolt is Zeus's chief weapon, made for him by the Cyclopes, and the symbol of his rule.
Bronze was the strongest metal known to the early Greeks, so it often marks things as solid and divine.
Poseidon, god of the sea and Zeus's brother, here helps secure the Titans' prison with bronze gates.
Sleep is gentle, while Death is pitiless; Hesiod makes both children of Night.

literary_notes.text: Sea, earth, Heaven and Olympus roar, groan and reel like living beings, showing the whole cosmos taking part in the battle.
Thick-flying bolts, thunder and whirling flame create a vivid sight and sound picture of Zeus's overwhelming power.
The din is compared to Earth and Heaven colliding, an exaggeration conveying a cosmic-scale clash.
"Until then" hints that the deadlock is about to end and the Titans' defeat is coming.
The anvil falling nine days and nights conveys the immense depth of Tartarus, as far below earth as earth is below heaven.
Night spreading like a neck-circlet gives the vast cosmic enclosure a familiar image of encircling.
Night and Day greet each other at the threshold like neighbors, turning the cycle of time into a meeting.
Death's heart of iron and spirit of bronze express his unyielding cruelty, contrasting with kindly Sleep.
